The base-rate prior strongly favors AAC over rarer alternatives (e.g., xanthogranulomatous cholecystitis, primary gallbladder lymphoma, or hepatic abscess), none of which typically present with isolated pericholecystic fluid + wall thickening *without stones* in this clinical context.

[EVIDENCE]  
- Altered mental status — a recognized risk factor for AAC (e.g., due to sepsis, metabolic encephalopathy, or immobility)  
- RUQ abdominal discomfort  
- RUQ tenderness on physical examination  
- Palpable RUQ mass — consistent with distended, inflamed gallbladder  
- Abdominal ultrasound shows pericholecystic fluid  
- Abdominal ultrasound shows gallbladder wall thickening (>3 mm)  
- Abdominal ultrasound confirms absence of gallstones  
- No jaundice, ascites, or peritoneal signs — making alternative diagnoses (e.g., cirrhosis, peritonitis, obstructive jaundice) less likely  

[GAPS]  
- Serum liver enzymes (ALT, AST, ALP, GGT) and bilirubin — needed to assess for concomitant hepatocellular injury or cholestasis  
- White blood cell count and CRP — to gauge inflammatory burden and sepsis risk  
- Common bile duct (CBD) diameter — unmeasured; critical to rule out coexisting choledocholithiasis or stricture  
- Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI — pending; would clarify complications (e.g., abscess, perforation, emphysematous changes) or alternative pathology  

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Acute acalculous cholecystitis
